prompt: Which pope carried out the first securely documented papal canonization, that of Ulrich of Augsburg in 993?
explanation: John XV canonized Ulrich in 993. Alexander III and Gregory IX came later and turned papal control of canonization into law.

prompt: When Christopher's feast was removed from the General Roman Calendar in 1969, the Catholic Church declared that he was no longer a saint.
explanation: Only his place on the universal calendar changed. Christopher stayed in the Roman Martyrology on 25 July and may still be honored locally.

prompt: What is the popular nickname for the Promoter of the Faith, the official who raised objections in canonization causes?
explanation: The Promoter of the Faith (promotor fidei) was nicknamed the devil's advocate (advocatus diaboli) because he argued against the candidate.

prompt: What did Pope Sixtus V create in 1588?
explanation: His bull Immensa Aeterni Dei set up the Congregation of Rites, which handled both liturgy and the causes of saints.

prompt: The inscription on Philomena's tomb tiles read PAX TECUM FILUMENA only after the tiles were rearranged.
explanation: As found, the tiles read LUMENA PAXTE CUMFI. Reordered, they gave 'peace be with you, Philomena,' which Marucchi later argued came from an older grave.

prompt: What did John Paul II's 1983 reform of the canonization process change?
options: It replaced courtroom-style debate with a historical dossier and reduced the miracles required
It abolished all miracle requirements for every candidate
It returned the power to canonize to local bishops
It created the Congregation of Rites
correctAnswer: It replaced courtroom-style debate with a historical dossier and reduced the miracles required
explanation: Divinus perfectionis Magister made the positio, a historical dossier, central, cut the promoter's prosecuting role, and in practice lowered the miracle count to one per stage.

prompt: Match each date to the event:

pairs.right: Audivimus placed in Gregory IX's Liber Extra
Congregation of Rites created by Sixtus V
Philomena's feast removed from all calendars

explanation: These dates trace how canonization moved from local practice to papal law and a Roman bureaucracy that could also withdraw cults.

prompt: Find the error in this account of how saints are made:
steps: Early martyr cults grew up around graves, with local bishops approving them
Alexander III objected to the cult of a man who had been killed while drunk
Gregory IX's Liber Extra of 1234 made papal reservation part of Church law
Urban VIII's 1634 constitution allowed any bishop to canonize saints in his own diocese
The 1969 calendar revision left Christopher in the Roman Martyrology
explanation: Step 4 is wrong. Caelestis Hierusalem cives did the opposite: it reserved beatification and canonization to the Holy See and banned public cult of unapproved persons.

prompt: What kind of animal was Saint Guinefort?
explanation: Guinefort was a greyhound. A mongoose plays the same role in the Sanskrit Panchatantra version of the tale.

prompt: Which Dominican friar wrote the only medieval account of the Guinefort cult?
explanation: Stephen of Bourbon (died c. 1261) described the cult in his handbook of exempla for preachers, in a section on superstition.

prompt: In the legend, the greyhound was killed by its master after it had saved the baby from a snake.
explanation: Finding the cradle overturned and the dog bloody, the knight assumed the worst and killed it, then found the child safe and the snake dead.

prompt: According to Stephen, whom did the mothers call on to take back the sick child and return a healthy one?
explanation: The mothers asked the fauns to take back the sick child, which they said was the fauns' own. Stephen read these woodland spirits as demons.

prompt: How did Jean-Claude Schmitt interpret the mothers' rite?
options: As based on changeling belief, in which a sickly baby was thought to be a supernatural substitute
As a disguised form of Dominican preaching
As a fiction invented by Stephen of Bourbon
As a ritual imported from Wales along with the legend of Gelert
correctAnswer: As based on changeling belief, in which a sickly baby was thought to be a supernatural substitute
explanation: Schmitt read the rite as an attempt to force the spirits to exchange a changeling for the true child.

prompt: Stephen of Bourbon's destruction of the shrine ended the cult within a generation.
explanation: The cult outlived the ban by centuries. The last known visits to the wood date from around the 1930s or 1940s.

prompt: Match each version of the faithful-animal tale to its description:

pairs.right: Much later Welsh legend of a hound
Greyhound honored as a martyr near Lyon

explanation: Schmitt showed that the Guinefort legend belongs to an international tale of an animal wrongly killed after saving a child.

prompt: Find the error in this account of Saint Guinefort:
steps: Stephen of Bourbon was a Dominican who preached in the region of Lyon
He wrote that the dog's body was thrown into a well
He reported that mothers passed sick infants between two tree trunks
He had the dog's bones dug up and burned with the grove
The Church later canonized Guinefort and listed him in the Roman Martyrology
explanation: Step 5 is wrong. No pope or bishop ever recognized the dog; the cult survived only as unofficial local practice that the Church opposed.

prompt: What makes images of Wilgefortis so startling?
options: They show a crucified woman with a full beard
They show a saint carrying her own head
They show a saint with a dog's head
They show a skeleton holding a scythe
correctAnswer: They show a crucified woman with a full beard
explanation: Wilgefortis is depicted crowned, bearded and crucified, often with a fiddler at her feet.

prompt: Wilgefortis was formally canonized by a pope in the fourteenth century.
explanation: She was never formally canonized. She entered the Roman Martyrology in 1583 and was removed after the Second Vatican Council as a fictional figure.

prompt: What was Wilgefortis called in England?
explanation: As Uncumber she was asked to 'uncumber' women of their troubles, which popular jokes took to mean their husbands.

prompt: Which crucifix is most often proposed as the model for images of Wilgefortis?
explanation: Copies of the Lucca crucifix showed a crowned, bearded Christ in a long tunic, which northern viewers may have read as a woman.

prompt: In Thomas More's Dialogue Concerning Heresies, what did women offer to Uncumber?
explanation: The Messenger jokes that 'for a peck of oats' she will uncumber women of their husbands, perhaps by providing a horse to carry them to the devil.

prompt: The Lucca crucifix had its own legend of a minstrel who received a silver shoe, a story later told of Kümmernis.
explanation: The shared minstrel-and-shoe legend is one of the strongest links between the Volto Santo and the bearded woman saint.

prompt: Match each name of the bearded saint to where it was used:
explanation: The same crucified bearded woman took different names, and different specialties, across Europe.

prompt: Find the error in this account of Wilgefortis and the Volto Santo:
steps: The Volto Santo shows Christ alive, crowned and wearing a long tunic
Painted and carved copies of it spread far beyond Tuscany
Radiocarbon tests announced in 2020 dated it to the fifteenth century
Schnürer and Ritz argued in 1934 that northern viewers read such robed figures as a woman
A figure of Uncumber survives in Henry VII's Lady Chapel at Westminster Abbey
explanation: Step 3 is wrong. The 2020 tests pointed to the late eighth or early ninth century, far earlier than the older eleventh-to-thirteenth-century dating, though the results are debated.

prompt: What does the word cephalophore mean?
explanation: From Greek for 'head-carrier,' the term describes martyrs said to have carried their own severed heads.

prompt: Which patron saint of France is the most famous cephalophore?
explanation: Denis, bishop of Paris, was said to have walked from Montmartre carrying his head to his burial place.

prompt: Some Eastern Orthodox icons show Saint Christopher with the head of a dog.
explanation: These icons follow the Greek Passion, which makes him a cynocephalus from a tribe of cannibals.

prompt: Which ninth-century abbot of Saint-Denis identified the Paris martyr with Dionysius the Areopagite?
explanation: Hilduin wrote a new Passion in the 830s after Michael II's gift of the Dionysian treatises in 827. Abelard later questioned the identification.

prompt: According to one explanation, why did a head-carrying legend strengthen a church's claim to a saint's relics?
options: It showed the saint had chosen his own resting place
It proved the relics had been bought legally
It showed the saint had been canonized by the pope
It proved the head and body belonged to different martyrs
correctAnswer: It showed the saint had chosen his own resting place
explanation: A martyr who walked to a spot and lay down there had, in effect, picked the shrine, a useful argument amid relic thefts and rival claims.

prompt: Russian icon painters made dog-headed Christophers with full church approval until the twentieth century.
explanation: A Russian church synod banned the dog-headed image in 1722. Old Believers, who rejected the official church's reforms, kept painting it.

prompt: Match each head-carrying saint to the place linked with them:
explanation: Head-carrying legends cluster in France but appear across Europe, often explaining the site of a major church.

prompt: Find the error in this account of Saint Denis:
steps: Gregory of Tours says Denis was bishop of Paris and was beheaded
In 827 Michael II sent Louis the Pious treatises attributed to Dionysius the Areopagite
Abbot Hilduin identified the Paris martyr with the Areopagite
Peter Abelard defended the identification and was honored by the monks for it
Scholars now distinguish the Areopagite, the bishop of Paris and Pseudo-Dionysius
explanation: Step 4 is wrong. Abelard questioned the identification around 1121 and had to flee the abbey of Saint-Denis.

prompt: What Greek word described a holy fool in Byzantium?
explanation: Salos means roughly 'crazy.' Yurodivy is the later Russian term for the same kind of saint.

prompt: What Russian word refers to a holy fool?
explanation: The yurodivy was a fool for Christ; the Russian Orthodox Church counts 36 of them among its saints.

prompt: According to his Life, Symeon of Emesa entered the city dragging a dead dog.
explanation: Leontius of Neapolis describes this entrance, which set the tone for Symeon's deliberately shocking behavior in Emesa.

prompt: What was the Red Square church now called Saint Basil's built to commemorate?
options: Ivan the Terrible's capture of Kazan
The end of the Time of Troubles
correctAnswer: Ivan the Terrible's capture of Kazan
explanation: Built in 1555 to 1561, it celebrated the capture of Kazan in 1552. Basil's name came from the chapel added over his grave in 1588.

prompt: Which feast, whose name the Red Square church officially bears, rests on a vision in the Life of Andrew the Fool?
explanation: In the Life, Andrew sees Mary spreading her veil over worshippers at Blachernae. The church is officially the Cathedral of the Intercession on the Moat.

prompt: Historians accept as fact the story that Ivan the Terrible blinded the architects of Saint Basil's.
explanation: Most historians regard it as a myth, since the builder appears in later records working on other projects.

prompt: Match each holy fool to a detail of their story:

pairs.right: Threw nuts at women in church
Rebuked Ivan the Terrible for inattention at the liturgy
Confronted Ivan during the campaign of 1570

explanation: Each fool broke social rules in public, but the details reflect very different settings, from a Syrian city to imperial Russia.

prompt: Find the error in this account of holy fools:
steps: Paul called the apostles 'fools for Christ's sake'
Leontius of Neapolis wrote the Life of Symeon of Emesa in the mid seventh century
The Life of Andrew the Fool is probably a tenth-century literary creation
Procopius of Ustyug was the first Russian holy fool to be canonized
Church councils consistently praised feigned madness as a path to holiness
explanation: Step 5 is wrong. Authorities were wary: the Council in Trullo (692) penalized those who feigned demonic possession, and Peter the Great's reforms treated many fools as impostors.

prompt: Whose life story lies behind the legend of Saint Josaphat?
explanation: Barlaam and Josaphat is a Christianized version of the Buddha's renunciation, carried west through Arabic, Georgian, Greek and Latin.

prompt: Josaphat's name derives ultimately from which Sanskrit word?
explanation: Bodhisattva became Arabic Budasaf, then Yudasaf through a misplaced dot, Greek Ioasaph and Latin Josaphat.

prompt: Saint Expedite is popularly invoked for urgent causes.
explanation: His name, from Latin expeditus ('prompt'), made him the saint for matters that cannot wait.

prompt: In images of Saint Expedite, what does the crow's banner say?
explanation: The crow says cras, which imitates its call, while the saint's cross reads hodie: do not put off until tomorrow what belongs to today.

prompt: In which Mexican city is Jesús Malverde's chapel?
explanation: Malverde is the 'angel of the poor' of Culiacán, the capital of Sinaloa, where his chapel draws a wide range of devotees.

prompt: Historians have found records showing that Jesús Malverde was executed in 1909.
explanation: No contemporary record of Malverde has been found. The 1909 date is traditional, and he may be a blend of two documented bandits.

prompt: Match each figure to how scholars explain the origin of their cult:

pairs.right: A Christianized life of the Buddha
A Latin word for a cloak turned into a name
A legend perhaps blending two Sinaloan bandits

explanation: Saints can be born from cross-cultural borrowing, copying errors, misread words or local legend.

prompt: Find the error in this account of Barlaam and Josaphat:
steps: The Arabic Kitab Bilawhar wa-Budasaf was current in eighth-century Baghdad
Euthymius of Athos is now generally credited with the Greek text
Marco Polo recognized that Saint Josaphat was the Buddha
Laboulaye and Liebrecht established the link in 1859 and 1860
The Greek church commemorates Barlaam and Josaphat on 26 August
explanation: Step 3 is wrong. Marco Polo praised the Buddha as someone who would have been a great saint had he been Christian, but he did not connect him to Josaphat.
